scenario_stem:
Renwick Precision Ltd is a private limited company that manufactures metal brackets and gear housings for agricultural machinery in Country X. The business employs 18 workers and has supplied two tractor assemblers for the past 6 years. Sales revenue is $640,000, and margins have narrowed as steel costs rose by 12% this year. Owner Priya Raman wants to buy a CNC machining centre costing $80,000 to win a new contract worth $150,000 a year.

Priya is comparing two external sources of finance. She could use factoring of debts: her debtors currently owe Renwick $100,000, and a factor has offered an immediate advance of 80% of the invoices ($80,000) in return for a 3% fee of $3,000. Alternatively, she could launch a crowdfunding campaign on an online platform, targeting $85,000; the platform charges a 5% fee ($4,250) and she must film promotional videos and send rewards to backers. Renwick has no other finance available now.

questions.model_answer: Factoring of debts is when a business sells its unpaid customer invoices (debtors) to a specialist finance company, which pays an immediate cash advance and then collects the money owed, usually in return for a fee. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Selling unpaid invoices/debtors to a specialist company (factor)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Renwick Precision Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Factoring releases cash immediately [k], so Renwick receives the $80,000 advance now instead of waiting for debtors to pay the $100,000 they owe, allowing it to buy the CNC machining centre costing $80,000 [app]. Advantage 2: The factor takes over chasing and collecting the debts [k], saving Renwick's 18 workers time and effort so that Priya Raman can concentrate on the new contract worth $150,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Immediate cash advance against unpaid invoices
Factor handles collection/credit control of the debts
application_max_2: CNC machining centre costing $80,000 / contract worth $150,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of crowdfunding for Renwick Precision Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The campaign may fail to reach its target [k]; Priya needs $85,000, and if pledges fall short the platform returns all the money, leaving Renwick unable to buy the CNC machining centre [app] and in no position to accept the new contract worth $150,000 a year [an]. Disadvantage 2: Running the campaign costs time and money [k]; Priya must film promotional videos, send rewards to backers and pay the 5% fee ($4,250) [app], distracting her from the core business and reducing the net cash raised [an].

knowledge_max_2: Funds returned if target not reached / no guarantee of raising the money

questions.question_text: Do you think Renwick Precision Ltd should use factoring of debts or crowdfunding? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Factoring has clear advantages: Renwick would receive the $80,000 advance immediately, the factor collects the $100,000 owed, and the fee is only $3,000 (3%) [k] [app]; the certainty suits a business that cannot wait for its debtors to pay [an]. However, Renwick loses some control over how customers are chased, and the advance leaves less margin on the invoices it sells [an]. Crowdfunding could raise the full $85,000 and build a public profile, but success is not guaranteed and the 5% fee costs $4,250 before rewards are sent to backers [k] [app]. Overall, I think Renwick should use factoring [eval], because the $3,000 fee is cheaper than the $4,250 crowdfunding fee and the $80,000 advance is far more certain; crowdfunding remains a useful fallback if Renwick cannot afford the immediate loss of margin [eval].

Crowdfunding could raise $95,000, more than the project costs, and would build publicity for the lodge [k], but the target is not guaranteed, the 5% fee costs $4,750 and plaques and discounted stays must be produced and honoured [app] [an]. Overall, I think Coveside should accept the grant [eval], because it is cheaper and far less risky given the certain $14,000 yearly saving; crowdfunding could complement it later to finance a wider eco-project, such as a wildlife garden, building on the publicity the solar panels attract [eval].

scenario_stem:
Stanway Uniform Co is a clothing manufacturer in Country X that supplies school and hospital uniforms, employing 30 full-time production workers. Monthly wage costs alone are $28,000, and annual sales revenue is $690,000. Its long-standing retail clients buy on 75-day credit terms and currently owe $84,000. Owner Ruth Calloway urgently needs to buy new embroidery machines costing $58,000 to keep a hospital contract worth $120,000 a year.

Ruth is comparing two external sources of finance. A factoring company will advance 90% of the outstanding invoices ($75,600) immediately, for a 2% fee ($1,680), and will take over credit control. Alternatively, a micro-finance institution offers a $25,000 loan at 13% annual interest over 3 years, costing $3,250 a year and $9,750 in total interest.

questions.question_text: Define 'debtor'.
questions.model_answer: A debtor is a customer or organisation that owes money to a business, usually because goods or services were bought on credit and payment has not yet been made. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Owes money to the business
Bought on credit / payment not yet received

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring of debts for Stanway Uniform Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Immediate cash is received [k]; 90% of the $84,000 owed ($75,600) is paid now, enough to buy the $58,000 embroidery machines without waiting 75 days [app]. Advantage 2: The factor takes over collecting the debts [k], removing the chasing workload from Ruth Calloway's 30 workers and helping to safeguard the hospital contract worth $120,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Immediate cash advance from outstanding invoices
Factor takes over debt collection/credit control

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Stanway Uniform Co.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The loan is far too small [k]; at $25,000 it leaves a $33,000 shortfall against the $58,000 machines [app], so the hospital contract worth $120,000 a year could be lost [an]. Disadvantage 2: Interest is expensive relative to the amount borrowed [k]; 13% costs $3,250 a year and $9,750 over 3 years [app], a heavy strain alongside monthly wages of $28,000 [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loan size limited / below requirements
Interest must be paid / cost of borrowing
analysis_max_2: Shortfall risks losing the hospital contract and revenue
Interest burden squeezes profit and cash flow alongside wages

questions.question_text: Do you think Stanway Uniform Co should use factoring of debts or micro-finance? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Factoring of debts [k] provides $75,600 now, comfortably covering the $58,000 machines, at a fee of only $1,680 (2%), and hands the slow 75-day collections to a specialist—but Stanway loses some control over how its hospital and school clients are dealt with, and confidential invoice information is disclosed to the factor [app] [an]. Micro-finance would keep Stanway in full control of its customer relationships [k], but it supplies only $25,000, leaving a $33,000 gap, and costs $9,750 in interest over 3 years on top of $28,000 monthly wages [app] [an]. Overall, I think Stanway should use factoring of debts [eval], because the machines cannot wait and the fee is small beside a $120,000-a-year contract; micro-finance would make sense only if Stanway later improved collections and wanted to avoid further fees [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Factoring: immediate advance, fee, confidentiality/control lost
Micro-finance: keeps control, smaller amount, interest
analysis_max_2: Speed and sufficiency vs cost and control
Effect on customer relationships, interest burden and profit
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing both sources with stem figures
Recognition of when micro-finance might be preferable / justified overall judgement

scenario_stem:
The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd runs a cafe and events hall in Country X, hosting 140 events a year and employing 12 staff. Annual sales revenue is $330,000, but the kitchen is worn out and the outdoor terrace is closed. The board of directors wants $30,000 for a new kitchen and terrace refurbishment, which should allow 40 extra events a year.

Two external sources of finance are being compared. A crowdfunding campaign, 'Save the Glasshouse', targets $35,000; the platform charges a 5% fee ($1,750) and rewards include a name on the wall and free dinners for donors. Alternatively, the government community regeneration subsidy offers $20,000, with the venue funding the remaining $10,000; in return, local groups get two free days of hall hire per month for 3 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'cash flow'.
questions.model_answer: Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over a period of time; the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Movement of money into and out of a business
Over a period of time / difference between inflows and outflows

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of crowdfunding for The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No interest or repayments are owed [k]; if the 'Save the Glasshouse' campaign reaches $35,000, the kitchen and terrace are funded by the community rather than by borrowing [app]. Advantage 2: The campaign raises publicity and loyalty [k]; reward donors, with their names on the wall and free dinners, are likely to become regulars, supporting the 140 events a year and $330,000 revenue [app].

Publicity/marketing benefit / community buy-in
application_max_2: $35,000 target funds the $30,000 kitchen and terrace

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the community regeneration subsidy for The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Binding conditions are attached [k]; local groups must get two free days of hall hire per month for 3 years [app], which could displace paying events and reduce the income needed to cover the cost of the 40 extra events [an]. Disadvantage 2: Only part of the cost is covered [k]; the subsidy gives $20,000, leaving the venue to find $10,000 itself [app], and any delay in grant approval could postpone the kitchen and terrace rebuild [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think The Glasshouse Community Venue Ltd should use crowdfunding or the subsidy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Crowdfunding [k] could raise $35,000, more than the $30,000 project, with no repayment, and the campaign would rally the local community behind the venue; however, reaching the target is not guaranteed, the 5% fee is $1,750, and free dinners and wall plaques must be produced [app] [an]. The subsidy is certain at $20,000 and non-repayable [k], but leaves a $10,000 gap and requires two free days of hall hire per month for 3 years, which could cost far more in lost bookings [app] [an]. Overall, I think The Glasshouse should use crowdfunding [eval], because the community goodwill, full funding and avoidance of restrictive hire conditions outweigh the uncertain target, provided the board markets the campaign strongly; if it fails, the subsidy can be claimed as a backup [eval].
